Construction of atomically dispersed Cu-N4 sites via engineered coordination environment for high-efficient CO2 electroreduction Huiyuan Chenga, Xuemei Wua,⁎, Xiangcun Lia, Xiaowa Nieb, Shuai Fana, Manman Fenga, Zihao Fana, Mingqian Tana, Yonggang Chenc, Gaohong Hea,⁎
a State Key Laboratory of Fine Chemicals, Research and Development Center of Membrane Science and Technology, School of Chemical Engineering, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian 116024, China b School of Chemical Engineering, PSU-DUT Joint Center for Energy Research, State Key Laboratory of Fine Chemicals, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian 116024, China cNetwork and Informationization Center, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian 116024, China
H I G H L I G H T S
• Highly exposed isolated Cu-Nx sites were embedded in microporous carbon frameworks. • CO2-to-CO conversion was boosted with tailored Cu–N coordination environment. • Cu-N4 exhibited a maximum FECO of 98% and over 90% from −0.6 to −1.1 V vs. RHE. • Edge-hosted Cu-N4 was identified as the accurate configuration of active site by DFT calculations.
G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T
Table of contents for mechanism model of Cu-N3 and Cu-N4 moieties.
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: CO2 electroreduction Single atom catalyst Coordination environment Electrochemical hydrogen pump reactor Density Functional Theory (DFT)
A B S T R A C T
Although considerable progress has been achieved by Cu nanoparticles for catalyzing CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR), Cu single atom catalysts (Cu SACs) are generally suffered from inferior performance to that of widely investigated Fe, Co, Ni SACs. This phenomenon mainly ascribes to the lack of effective geometry and electronic engineering of copper active center from an atomic level. Herein, highly exposed atomically dispersed Cu-Nx (x denotes Cu–N coordination number) sites anchored on 3D porous carbon matrix are successfully synthesized through facile one step thermal activation, and Cu-N4 sites exhibit boosted activity and selectivity compared to its nearly inert Cu-N3 counterparts. Aided by density functional theory (DFT) calculations, the edge-hosted Cu-N4 moieties are revealed as key active sites for efficient CO generation via optimized local coordination environment and electronic properties, which strongly interact with *COOH intermediate and facilitate the desorption of *CO. As a result, Cu-N4 catalyst achieves high CO Faradaic efficiency (FECO) of over 90% from −0.6 to −1.1 V vs. RHE with a maximum value of 98%, surpassing the previously reported Cu SACs for CO2-to-CO conversion. This work provides new insight into proper Cu SACs design and fundamental mechanism understanding to boost CO2RR.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The excessive consumption of fossil fuels results in both energy crisis and global warming effect by huge CO2 emission [1]. Therefore, direct CO2 electrochemical conversion coupled with renewable energybased electricity provides a clean and controllable strategy to mitigate CO2 accumulation and yield value-added chemicals [2–6]. Among the various kinds of CO2RR products, CO features advantages of low electron consumption, relatively rapid reaction kinetics and compatibility with Fischer-Tropsch synthesis for fundamental organic chemicals [7].
Noble metals (e.g., Au, [8–10] Ag, [11,12] and Pd [13]) are wellknown electrocatalysts for their excellent CO2-to-CO performances, for example, ∼100% CO selectivity was observed on Au25[8]. However, their high cost and scarcity set great limitations to its industry-scale application [14]. As a popular earth-abundant metal, Cu can electrochemically convert CO2 into a variety of chemicals, including CO, hydrocarbons, and alcohols. Although tremendous efforts have been taken into development of Cu-based catalysts, the synchronized complexity originated from diverse lattice planes, polycrystalline vacancies, defects and chemical states results in low CO selectivity and high overpotential [15,16]. Hence exert great obstacle to correlate between structure of active sites and catalytic performances.
Recently, single atom catalysts (SACs) combining the merits of heterogeneous and homogeneous catalysts exhibit superior performances in CO2RR due to well-defined single atomic sites [17]. The definite structure of active site makes it possible for exploring the structure–activity relationship and rational design of the targeted catalysts [18–20]. Moreover, the catalytic performances of SACs can be tuned through precisely modulating the electronic structure and coordination environment of central active sites [21,22]. Although remarkable activity and CO selectivity have been achieved on Fe [23–25], Co [26], Ni [27,28], Zn [29], Sn [30], and Sb [31] SACs for CO2RR, there are very few reports on Cu-based single atom materials in catalyzing CO2-to-CO and the performances are far from satisfactory. Ju and coworkers investigated various M−Nx moieties, including Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and observed that Cu–N-C only reached ∼30% CO selectivity at −0.75 V vs. RHE, inferior to Ni-N-C (85%, −0.78 V vs. RHE) [32]. Ding and coworkers demonstrated that without incorporation of Ni atom, Cu-C3N4-CNT showed ordinary selectivity for CO evolution (60%, −0.8 V vs. RHE) [33]. The low intrinsic activity of the above mentioned Cu SACs likely lies in unoptimized coordination environment of central active sites. And the correlation between local copper coordination structure versus CO2RR catalytic activity still remains to be elucidated. Zheng and coworkers reported Cu SACs comprising undercoordinated Cu-N2 sites anchored on graphene matrix [34]. The prepared catalyst showed much enhanced catalytic activity for CO selectivity of 81% at −0.5 V vs. RHE. However, the CO current efficiency drops rapidly with the increase of applied potential, which may probably relate to the comparatively small BET surface and lack of porous texture considering the 2D planar structure of graphene. To address this issue, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) derived SACs with tunable structure and interconnected carbon framework create a favorable microenvironment for modulating metal centers and promoting mass transfer [35], which facilitates the proper design of Cu-based materials from an atomic scale and rational construction of Cu active sites with optimum electronic structure.
Herein, we synthesized Cu SACs with highly exposed atomically dispersed Cu-Nx sites under the assistance of MOFs and correlated the underlying mechanism between local coordination environments of central copper sites with CO2RR catalytic activity. The coordination environment and electronic structure of central copper sites were tailored through facile one-step thermal activation under different pyrolysis temperatures. The catalyst with Cu-N4 sites (Cu-N4-C/1100) exhibits outstanding activity and selectivity for CO2-to-CO conversion compared to its Cu-N3 counterpart (Cu-N3-C/800), achieving high CO
Faradaic efficiency (FECO) of over 90% from −0.6 to −1.1 V vs. RHE and reaching a maximum FECO of 98% at −0.9 V vs. RHE. So far as we know, such a high CO selectivity is superior to the previously reported Cu SACs catalysts. Moreover, during 40-hour stability test, Cu-N4-C/ 1100 exhibited negligible FECO and current declination. Further density functional theory (DFT) calculations elucidated that through suitable interactions with *COOH and *CO intermediates, the edge-hosted CuN4 sites were suggested to be the more accurate configuration of copper active sites of Cu SACs.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: Zinc nitrate hexahydrate (Zn(NO3)2·6H2O) was obtained from Shandong West Asia Reagents, China. Copper acetate monohydrate (Cu (OAc)2·H2O) was purchased from Tianjin Guangfu Fine Chemical Research Institute, China. 2-methylimidazole (2-MeIM) was acquired from Aladdin. Methanol, Potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3), N,NDimethyl Formamide (DMF) and Isopropyl alcohol were obtained from Tianjin Chemical Reagent, China. Commercial 20% Pt/C obtained from Dalian Xinyuan Dongli, China. 5 wt% Nafion solution (Dupont) were purchased from Shanghai Hephas Energy Equipment, China.

sections.heading: 2.2. Catalysts synthesis
sections.text: In a typical procedure, a mixture of Zn(NO3)2·6H2O (11.9 g) and Cu (OAc)2·H2O (798.6mg) was dissolved in methanol (300mL) under vigorous stirring for 10min and ultrasound for 5min. The mixture was subsequently added into methanol (150mL) solution in which 2-MeIM (13.14 g) was dissolved. After stirring for 15min, the mixture was kept at room temperature without agitating for 12 h. Next, the Cu/Zn-ZIF nanoparticles (NPs) were collected by centrifugation (9000 rpm, 7min) and thoroughly washed with DMF and methanol for three times, and dried at 60 °C under vacuum overnight. Catalysts marked as Cu-Nx-C/T (x and T denote Cu–N coordination number and calcination temperature, respectively) were obtained through pyrolysis in the tube furnace and heated under certain temperature (800, 900, 1000, 1100 °C) for 3 h at a heating rate of 5 °Cmin−1 under Ar atmosphere. For comparison, N-C/800 and N-C/1100 was prepared through similar procedure to CuN3-C/800 and Cu-N4-C/1100, respectively, without adding Cu (OAc)2·H2O.

sections.heading: 2.3. CO2 electroreduction experiments
sections.text:
Electrocatalytic characterizations were conducted in a three-electrode setup connected to an electrochemical workstation (CHI760E). And the controlled-potential electrolysis was performed in an electrochemical hydrogen pump reactor at room temperature, which can be found in our earlier reports [36]. For preparation of CO2RR cathode, 15.0 mg sample and 80 μL Nafion (5wt%) were dispersed into 3mL isopropanol by sonication for at least 30min. The homogeneous ink was air-brushed onto 2.3 cm×2.3 cm carbon paper (Avcarb MB30), with catalyst loading of about 1.5mg cm−2. A Nafion 115 (Dupout) anionexchange membrane was hot pressed onto carbon paper with 0.5 mg cm−2Pt/C catalyst layer to form membrane electrode assembly (MEA), which served as a hydrogen oxidation anode. A flow of 20 sccm CO2(99.99%) and 30 sccm H2 (99.99%) were purged through cathode and anode gas diffusion layers, respectively. The cathode was circulated with 30mL 0.1M KHCO3 electrolyte at a flow rate of 15mLmin−1 through a peristaltic pump. According to the Nernst equation: E (vs. RHE)= E (vs. Ag/AgCl)+ 0.21 V+0.059× pH, all the measured potentials vs. Ag/AgCl reference electrode were converted to reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) reference scale [1]. The corresponding pH for the CO2-saturated 0.1, 0.5, 1.0M KHCO3 cathode electrolyte were measured to be 6.8, 7.2, and 7.8, respectively. For each applied
potential, 40min continuous electrolysis was conducted after CO2 saturation for at least 30min, the gas products (CO and H2) of CO2RR were online collected every 12min on Gas Chromatography (GC, Shimadzu GC-2014), which equipped with a molecular sieve-13X column, flame ionization detectors (FID) and a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). And the liquid products were collected after electrolysis, by using 50 μL 100 ppm Dimethyl sulphoxide (DMSO) as internal standard, 0.2 mL electrolyte with 0.4mL Deuterium oxide (D2O) was analyzed by H1 nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, Bruker AVANCE III 500MHz). And no liquid products were detected in this case. The calculation models of Faradaic efficiency (FE), CO partial current density (JCO), and mass loading normalized Turnover Frequency (TOF) for CO production can be found in Supplementary Materials. The electrochemical measurements were performed in gastight two-compartment glass cell. Carbon paper with 1.5 mg cm−2 catalyst loading was cut into 1 cm×1.25 cm, and used as working electrode, platinum wire and leak-free Ag/AgCl were served as counter and reference electrodes, respectively. Each compartment contained 30mL 0.1M KHCO3 electrolyte and separated by Nafion 115. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) tests were carried out in 0.1M KHCO3 solution saturated by Ar or CO2 with a scan rate of 5 mv s−1. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests were performed from the frequency value of 100 KHz to 100mHz with 5mV alternation voltage. Cyclic voltammograms (CV) measurements were performed in the potential range of 0.41 to 0.61 V at different scan rate (5, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50mV s−1), and the slope of current difference (Δj) between anode (ja) and cathode (jc) at 0.51 V plotted against the scan rate represented twice of the double layer capacitance (Cdl). As the roughness factor (Rf) positively related with Cdl, the electrochemical surface area (ECSA) can be obtained through the equation ECSA= Rf × Sg, where Sg denotes the geometric area of carbon paper electrode [14,37].

sections.heading: 2.4. Physical characterization
sections.text: Catalysts morphology was visualized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) on Nova NanoSEM NPE218 (FEI, USA) operated at a working voltage of 3 kV. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and Energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS) was performed on JEM2100F (JEOL, Japan) measured at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. High-angle annular dark field-scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) was carried out on JEM-ARM200F (JEOL, Japan). The crystal phase was examined by X-ray diffraction (XRD) on D/MAX-2400 with Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.5406 Å). Inductively coupled plasma (ICP) was performed on Optima 2000DV perkinelmer to detect mass content of Cu species and the sample was prepared by digestion in HClO4 and HNO3 mixture at 180 °C. Detailed surface chemical environment was analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) on ESCALAB 250Xi, Al Kα X-ray was adopted as exciting source. Raman spectrum was collected on Thermo Fisher DXR Smart Raman to evaluate the graphitizing extent. Nitrogen adsorption/desorption isotherms were measured on Autosorb-1-MP at 77 K, the porosity and specific surface area of as-prepared catalysts were investigated through BET analysis. The Cu K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) was detected at BL14W beamline in Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF). The storage ring of SSRF was operated at 3.5 GeV with a stable current of 200mA. The data were recorded under fluorescence mode with a Lytle detector and Cu foil was used as references recorded under transmission mode. Athena and Artemis were employed to normalize the profile and describe the local configuration environment.

sections.heading: 2.5. Computational methods
sections.text:
Spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT) calculations, including structure optimizations, single-point energies and electronic structures, were carried out by Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) [38]. The electron exchange and correlation energy were
described by the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional with a generalized gradient approximation (GGA) [39]. The DFT+D3 method developed by Grimme was employed to treat the Van der Waals interactions [40]. A 4× 4×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point sampling [41] of the Brillouin zone was adopted for the structure optimization and a 8×8×1 k-point sampling was used for the single-point energy and electronic structure calculations. The cutoff energy for plane-wave basis set was set to 500 eV. A vacuum space of 20 Å was added in the z direction (perpendicular to the catalyst surface) to avoid the interaction between periodic slabs. For the structure optimization, the total energy and force convergences were set to be smaller than 10−6 eV and 0.01 eV Å−1, respectively. Electronic smearing was used by the Gaussian-smearing scheme with a width of 0.05 eV. Partial charge transfers from the catalyst to intermediates (*COOH, *CO and *H, where the asterisk (*) represents a species bound to the catalyst surface) were evaluated by Bader charge analysis [42]. The Gibbs free energy change (ΔG) for all elemental steps was calculated based on the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) model, [43] which can be calculated as [44]
= + + + +( )G E ZPE C T T S G Gdp UpH =G k T2.303 ·pHBpH
=G zeUU
where T is the temperature, E represents the electronic energy, which is directly obtained from DFT calculations. ZPE indicates the zero point energy, which is calculated by (1/2)∑ℏν [45]. S is the entropy, which is obtained from the NIST database for the free molecules; meanwhile the vibration entropy of adsorbed species was taken into account. Cp is the constant pressure heat capacity. ΔGpH denotes the free energy change owing to the pH variation of solution [43]. Here, pH was set to 0 for a strong acidic solution, so the calculated applied potential was referenced to the RHE. ΔGU denotes the free energy change related to the electrode potential, where z was the number of electrons transferred and U is the electrode potential. According to Peterson’s paper [46], the solvation corrections were considered for Gibbs free energy (G) calculations of *COOH (0.25 eV) and *CO (0.1 eV). Moreover, due to the failure of traditional PBE exchange–correlation functional to describe the C=O double bond, the Gibbs free energies of CO2 and CO molecules in bulk gas were corrected by the value of 0.13 eV and −0.51 eV, respectively [46].

sections.heading: 3.1. Material analysis
sections.text:
The synthesis of Cu SACs is schematically illustrated in Fig. 1a. The Cu/Zn-ZIF was first prepared via in situ incorporation of Cu2+ into ZIF8 framework, which partially replaced Zn2+ nodes to coordinate with 2-MeIM. After pyrolysis at various temperatures (800, 900, 1000, and 1100 °C), Cu/Zn ZIF-8 were facilely transformed into Cu SACs with different Cu-Nx (x=3, 3.3, 3.8 and 4, accordingly) active sites anchored on 3D carbon matrix. Due to the immobilization effect by 2- MeIM [47] and the spatial disassembly effect by Zn nodes [48], Cu ions can directly transform to Cu SACs without Cu-Cu aggregation. As visualized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in Fig. 1b, c, Cu-N4-C/1100 Nanoparticles (NPs) inherited the rhombododecahedral shape of ZIF-8 and uniform in size about 100 nm, which had similar morphology to other prepared samples (Fig. S1). The energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS) images (Fig. 1d) revealed that Cu, C, and N atoms had homogeneous distributions throughout the polyhedron. As revealed by High-resolution TEM (HRTEM), the evaporation of Zn species leaves large abundant of micropores, resulting in highly disordered N-doped carbon rich in vacancies and dislocations (Fig. 1e and Fig. S2a) for anchoring of Cu atoms and no aggregated Cu particles appeared in the carbon structure.
Due to higher Z-contrast of Cu than non-metallic elements, high-angle annular dark field-scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADFSTEM) in sub-angstrom resolution verified the uniform dispersion of single Cu atoms, visualized by abundant scattered bright points (Fig. 1f). In addition, a plenty of Cu atoms anchored on the edge of carbon matrix is observed from HAADF-STEM image (Fig. S2b). The ring-like pattern, taken from selected area electron diffraction (SAED), revealed an amorphous character in absence of metal NPs (Fig. 1g) [49].
X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns coincided well with SAED results, no metallic phase was detected and the peaks at about 23° and 44° related to (002) and (101) plane of graphitic carbon (Fig. 2a) [50,51]. Raman spectra (Fig. S3) exhibited two typical graphitic D and G bands, which related to disorder or defect carbon and sp2-hybridized carbon, respectively [52,53]. As reflected from the reduced value of ID/IG and sharper shape of G peak, the graphitization degree was enhanced as carbonization temperature increases, which is in agreement with the previous reports [54–56]. By promoting electron transfer, the generation of graphitized carbon is favorable to CO2RR. The elemental compositions of Cu SACs were analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). As shown in Fig. S4a, Table S1, C, N, O, and Cu elements were presented in the as-prepared Cu-Nx-C/T samples and no significant Zn signals were detected in the Cu-N4-C/1100, demonstrating its sufficient evaporation under 1100 °C thermal treatment. Meanwhile, the Cu loading amount of Cu-N4-C/1100 was analyzed to be 1.98 wt% by inductively coupled plasma (ICP). The high-resolution N 1 s spectra of Cu-Nx-C/T were deconvoluted into five component peaks, representing pyridinic-N (398.2 eV), Cu–N (398.9 eV), pyrrolic-N
(400.5 eV), graphitic-N (401.3 eV), and oxidized-N (403.7 eV), [57–59] respectively. As observed from Fig. 2b, Cu-N4-C/1100 emerged an obvious Cu–N peak and showed similar ratios of pyrrolic-N and graphiticN compared with N-C/1100 (Table S2). Meanwhile, higher carbonization temperature brings about loss of N content, especially pyridinic-N, but more thermally stable and conductive graphitic-N. Notably, the Cu–N content increased from 15.5 to 20.4% as heating temperature enhanced from 800 to 1100 °C, further indicating the transition of Cu–N coordination of Cu-Nx sites. The XPS spectra of Cu 2p were shown in Fig. S4b, for the catalysts of Cu-N3-C/800 and Cu-N3.3-C/900, the characterized peaks at binding energies of 932.3 eV and 952.3 eV were assigned to Cu+ species, [58] and the peaks at 935.0 eV and 954.9 eV were related to Cu2+ species, [59,60] which emerged under higher carbonization temperature. The textural structure was further characterized by N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms (Fig. 2c). Benefitting from well-defined ZIF-8 precursors, Cu-N4-C/1100 exhibited a large BET surface area of 1347.1m2 g−1 and a total pore volume of 1.745 cm3 g−1 (Table S3). Moreover, the hierarchical porous structure demonstrated the active Cu-N4 site to be fully exposed where CO2 can be adsorbed and reduced (Fig. S5) [61]. Benefiting from reduced mass transfer resistance, hence ensure sufficient supply at higher reactant consumption.
To unravel the local structure properties of central Cu active sites, Cu K edge X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy (XANES) and extended X-ray fine structure (EXAFS) were examined. The near-edge adsorption energy of Cu SACs locates between Cu2O and CuO, confirming the Cu valence state is between+ 1 and+2 (Fig. 3a). As shown in Fig. S6, the fitted oxidation state of Cu atoms in Cu-Nx-C/T
Fig. 1. (a) Schematic description procedure for Cu-Nx-C/T. (b) SEM image, (c) TEM and (d) the corresponding EDS mapping of Cu-N4-C/1100. (e) HRTEM images, (f) HAADF-STEM images and (g) SAED pattern of Cu-N4-C/1100.
displayed an increase trend from 1.1 to 1.3, 1.8, and 1.9 for Cu-N3-C/ 800, Cu-N3.3-C/900, Cu-N3.8-C/1000, Cu-N4-C/1100, respectively, which indicates the transition of coordination environment of Cu atoms. Fourier transition of EXAFS curves of Cu SACs samples displayed the dominant peak at∼ 1.5 Å, which can be assigned to Cu–N or Cu–O coordination. And the Cu-Cu peak at 2.2 Å was not detected (Fig. 3b), confirming atomic dispersed of Cu species anchored on the N-C matrix [62]. To further discriminate the backscattering atoms, wavelet transform (WT) of EXAFS was employed for its efficiency in providing both k and R spaces resolution. The WT contour plots of Cu-N4-C/1100 exhibited intensity maximum at 3.89 Å−1, which was associated with Cu–N path, and clearly distinguished from Cu-O (4.4 Å−1) and Cu-Cu
(7.1 Å−1) coordination (Fig. 3c). The quantitative structural parameters can be obtained by EXAFS fitting (Fig. 3d, Figs. S7 and S8), and the results were listed in Table S3. The first shell of Cu-N3-C/800 and CuN4-C/1100 had the coordination numbers of 2.9 and 4, with the corresponding average bond lengths of 1.91 and 1.94 Å, respectively. As for Cu-N3.3-C/900 and Cu-N3.8-C/1000 with the average Cu–N coordination numbers of 3.3 and 3.8 virtually contain both Cu-N3 and CuN4 moieties, whereas, Cu-N3.8-C/1000 possessed a higher Cu-N4 content. The transition of coordination environment of Cu centers from CuN3 (800 °C) to Cu-N4 (1100 °C) probably resulted from the mobility of Cu atoms under higher calcination temperature to form a more stable Cu–N anchor structure.
Fig. 2. (a) XRD patterns, (b) high resolution N 1 s XPS spectra and (c) N2 adsorption–desorption isotherms of Cu-Nx-C/T and N-C/1100.

sections.heading: 3.2. CO2 electrocatalytic reduction
sections.text:
As revealed by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) in Fig. 4a, Cu-N4-C/ 1100 exhibited a rapid rise in current density and lower onset potential of −0.38 V vs. RHE compared with N-C/1100 (in view of the CO2/CO standard equilibrium potential of −0.11 V vs. RHE, [63,64] its onset overpotential equals to 270mV). And showed more negative the current density of Cu-N4-C/1100 measured in CO2-saturated electrolyte than that of Ar suggested the occurrence of CO2RR. The LSV comparisons of the prepared Cu SACs showed a larger current response with increasing Cu–N coordination number, indicating its positive effect on CO2RR activity (Fig. S9). To examine the cathode products and elucidate the corresponding selectivity, Faradaic efficiency (FE) was measured by conducting potentiostatic electrolysis in the electrochemical hydrogen pump reactor [36] equipped with a gas diffusion electrode (GDE). Detected by online GC and 1H NMR, CO and H2 were the only products for all the tested catalysts. Remarkably, Cu-N4-C/1100 achieved FECO of over 90% from −0.6 V vs. RHE onwards and reached a maximum value of 98% at −0.9 V vs. RHE, whereas N-C/1100 showed low FECO value (40% at −0.6 V vs. RHE) and its CO partial current density reached less than half of the value of Cu-N4-C/1100 at each measured potential (Fig. 4b), highlighting the crucial role of copper site in activation of CO2RR. In order to identify the relevance between copper coordination configuration and CO2RR catalytic performances, Cu SACs with different Cu–N coordination numbers were evaluated. As presented in Fig. 4c, the FECO witnessed a sharp increase from nearly inert (21%) to approaching 100% at −0.7 V vs. RHE as Cu–N coordination increased from 3 to 4. Likely, the corresponding CO partial current density dramatically boosted from 0.1 to 3.3 mA cm−2
(Fig. S10a). As revealed from the calculated FE of H2 (Fig. S10b), the total FE for gaseous products (CO and H2) was measured to be around 100% and no liquid products were detected (Fig. S10c). Notably, the large FECO of Cu-N4-C/1100 maintained at even higher overpotential, which benefits from the fully exposed active sites for the occurrence of CO2RR and efficient mass transfer, owing to the 3D porous structure and sufficient reactant supply by GDE. In addition, the calculated TOFs reached 1012 h−1 for Cu-N4-C/1100 at −0.8 V vs. RHE according to the loading content of Cu atoms (Fig. S10d). To further confirm the catalytic activity of Cu-N4 sites and distinguishing the contribution of N-C
sites, poisoning experiment was performed by introducing SCN− into to the electrolyte [34,65]. As shown in Fig. S11, the poisoned Cu-N4-C/ 1100 only reaches FECO of 41% at −0.7 V vs. RHE, along with sharp decrease in CO current density. Thus the obvious restrained CO2RR performance further demonstrate the vital role of Cu-N4 sites. Moreover, as the transition of local coordination of Cu atoms resulted in change of Cu oxidation state, there observed clear increase trend of FECO with the increase of the valence state of Cu atoms in Cu-Nx-C/T (Fig. S12a), which strongly supports the essential effect of Cu–N coordination number on the catalytic activity of CO2RR. However, the Zn loading amount displayed a sharp decrease from 12.54 to 0.13 wt% (ICP) with little impact on catalytic performance of Cu SACs (Fig. S12b) and the lowered activity and selectivity of N-C/800 compared with Cu–N-C/800 further demonstrate negligible catalytic activity of Zn species towards CO2RR in our work (Fig. S12c and d). In this case, the remarkable enhancement of catalytic activity and selectivity of Cu-N4C/1100 were likely derived from the synergistic effect between Cu and doped N in forming Cu-N4 moieties. Furthermore, Cu-N4-C/1100 exhibited excellent stability during electrolysis, as presented in Fig. 4d, negligible decrease in current density after 40-hour continuous potentiostatic test with CO selectivity maintained∼97%. In addition, HAADF-STEM and the corresponding EDS images also demonstrated the robust nature of Cu single sites under electrolysis conditions as observed by the well dispersed Cu atoms after 40-hour stability test (Fig. S13). As presented in Fig. S14 by increasing the concentration of KHCO3 electrolyte, the maximum of FECO appeared at even lower overpotential and CO production rate increased from 0.06mmol h−1 cm−2 at −0.70 V vs. RHE (0.1M KHCO3) to 0.175mmol h−1 cm−2 at −0.74 V vs. RHE (1M KHCO3). To the best of our knowledge, such intriguing CO2-to-CO performance of Cu-N4-C/1100 has seldom been reached by the previously reported Cu SACs and benchmark well with the high-performance CO2RR catalysts, as listed in Table S5.

sections.heading: 3.3. Mechanistic study
sections.text:
To further investigate CO2 electroreduction on Cu SACs from a kinetic perspective, Tafel analysis was carried out in the CO formation pathway as illustrated in Fig. 4e. Cu-N4-C/1100 showed favorable kinetics for CO formation as evidenced by the smallest Tafel slope of
Fig. 4. (a) The LSV curves of Cu-N4-C/1100 and N-C/1100 measured in Ar-saturated 0.1M phosphate buffer (PBS, pH=6.8) and CO2-saturated 0.1M KHCO3 (pH=6.8), (b) CO Faradaic efficiency and CO current density of Cu-N4-C/1100 and N-C/1100, (c) CO Faradaic efficiency of Cu-Nx-C/T at various applied potentials measured in CO2-saturated 0.1M KHCO3, (d) Cu-N4-C/1100 stability test at −0.8 V vs. RHE for 40-hour continuous potentiostatic test, (e) Tafel plots for CO partial current density and (f) Nyquist plots of as-prepared catalysts.
113mV dec−1, which approached the theoretical value of 118mV dec−1. It indicates the formation of surface adsorbed COOH* intermediates possibly the rate-determining step [37,66]. Meanwhile, such fast electron transfer capacity was also witnessed by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) (Fig. 4f). Cu-N4-C/1100 displayed the lowest charge transfer resistance (Rct), hence facilitating the kinetics of CO2·− generation [37,67]. Notably, Nyquist plots of N-C/1100 showed similar semicircle as Cu-N4-C/1100, suggested that high conductivity partly improved catalytic activity but was not a limiting factor. Furthermore, the slope of log (jCO) plotted against log ([HCO3−]) displayed a slope of 0.44 (Fig. S15). The first-order dependence of reduction rate on HCO3− demonstrates that HCO3− may participate in both proton donations during CO2RR and increase of CO2 concentration though equilibrium with bicarbonate [29,68,69]. The electrochemical surface area (ECSA) was measured through double-layer capacitance (Cdl), calculating from cyclic voltammetry (CV) [70,71]. As shown in Fig. S16, Cu-N4-C/1100 exhibited an enhanced Cdl value of 63.27 mF cm−2 compared with the other prepared Cu SACs, which consequently provided sufficient area to support more active sites. However, as visualized by similar Cdl value of Cu-N3.3-C/900 and Cu-N3.8-C/1000 but significant difference in CO2-to-CO performances, the intrinsic activity of active sites may play a key role during the CO2RR process. The same conclusion can also be drawn from comparing Cdl value of Cu-N4-C/ 1100 with N-C/1100.

sections.heading: 3.4. DFT calculations of the CO2 electroredution activity
sections.text:
To provide theoretical insight into understanding the origin of enhanced CO2RR performance of Cu-N4-C/1100 and the reactivity nature of different N-coordination sites, DFT calculations were conducted according to the fitting results obtained from EXAFS data. The various optimized catalyst models are illustrated in Fig. 5a. Previous studies have suggested that CO2-to-CO reaction generally undergo couple proton-electron transfer through successively generating *COOH and *CO intermediates [63,67,72]. The calculated free energy diagrams were plotted in Fig. 5b. It showed that CO2 activation (*COOH formation) was an endothermic process for both Cu-N4 (CuN4bulk and Cu-N4edge) and N-C sites. Compared with N-C site, the introduction of Cu-N4 active site substantially lowered the energy barrier
for *COOH formation, thus showing lowered onset potential and enhanced performance. Considering the competitive H2 evolution reaction (HER), via calculating the limiting potentials of CO2RR (UL(CO2), UL= −ΔG0/e) and HER (UL(H2)), the higher CO selectivity was evidenced by the more positive value of UL(CO2) −UL(H2) [67,73,74]. In this case, only Cu-N4 presented a positive value compared to Cu-N3 and N-C moieties (Fig. 5c and Fig. S17), indicating the ability to suppress HER and boost CO production. Although Cu-N3 exhibited a downhill free-energy pathway for CO2 activation, it showed much negative free energy than other moieties for the generation of *CO via second protonelectron transfer. This poisoning effect caused by strong *CO affinity significantly limited the CO desorption step on Cu-N3 and thus detrimental to CO2RR performance. This phenomenon was also confirmed by the nearly inert activity gained from experimental results.
For the subtle structure of Cu-N4, it could be either embedded in the bulk (Cu-N4bulk) or at the edge (Cu-N4edge) of the carbon matrix [75]. It is requisite to identify these two moieties as real active sites. As observed in Fig. 5b, the barrier of CO2-to-*COOH for Cu-N4bulk is 1.41 eV, when the negative potential of −1.41 V vs. RHE is applied on Cu-N4bulk, all the reaction steps are energetically downhill for CO2-to-CO conversion. The corresponding potential is positively shifted to −0.9 V vs. RHE for Cu-N4edge moieties, suggesting a much easier protonation process to form *COOH is verified for Cu-N4edge (Fig. S18). This is also consistent with a larger charge transfer from the catalyst to *COOH (0.396 e−) through Bader charge analysis, shorter Cu-C (*COOH) bond (1.92 Å) and elongated C-O bond (1.38 Å) where C-O cleavage to form *CO. The corresponding value for Cu-N4bulk is 0.340 e−, 1.96 Å, and 1.37 Å, respectively (Fig. 5d, e). In addition, the analysis of the partial density of state (PDOS) (Fig. S19) revealed that the d-band center of CuN4edge was much closer to Fermi level than Cu-N4bulk (−2.58 eV vs. −3.59 eV), and the consequently lower occupation of antibonding orbital with *COOH adsorbed further supports the strong binding interactions and more stabilized adsorption on Cu-N4edge. Therefore, through the examination of reaction energetic paths and electronic property analysis, the Cu-N4 moieties embedded at the edge of the carbon matrix were the most possible configuration of active sites.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, we have successfully developed atomically dispersed Cu electrocatalysts with different Cu–N coordination environments through MOF assisted synthesis strategy. The structural characterizations by HAADF-STEM, HRTEM, EDS, XPS, and XAFS demonstrate the uniform dispersion of copper atoms in the nitrogen-doped porous carbon matrix. As the Cu–N coordination number increases to 4, the catalytic activity and selectivity were significantly promoted. The CuN4 site endows Cu SACs with high FECO of over 90% in a wide potential range at a moderate overpotential. DFT calculations revealed that the superior activities of Cu-N4 sites mainly originate from the appropriate binding energy strength of *COOH and *CO species, thus enhancing CO generation. Moreover, the edge-hosted Cu-N4edge with d-band center much closer to the Fermi level exhibited a lower energy barrier for *COOH formation as compared to its bulk-hosted counterpart, thus was identified to be the active site for CO2RR. This work highlights the vital role of designing and engineering the coordination environment of Cu center from an atomic level and would open a new avenue to the development of Cu SACs for CO2 reduction.
